analysis.one_liner: Creates universal federally funded child care and early learning for children from six weeks old until school age.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and received no hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made child care and early learning available to every child from six weeks of age until the age a state requires school attendance, regardless of family income, disability status, or citizenship status. Families below 200% of the poverty line would pay nothing; other families would pay a sliding fee capped at 7% of household income, with the federal government covering most of the cost. The program would run through states, cities, tribal organizations, and nonprofits, and would set national quality standards, a wage and bargaining process for child care workers, and an individual entitlement for each covered child. It never advanced past its initial referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children — including low-income families, children with disabilities, migrant farmworker families, and families regardless of citizenship status — would get access to affordable, full-working-day, year-round child care and early learning. Child care and early learning workers would gain required compensation levels, career pathways, and a collective process to set wages and working conditions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and child care workers

how_it_helps.text: Every covered child would hold an individual, uncapped entitlement to participate in a program meeting the bill's requirements, regardless of family income, disability status, citizenship status, or whether a family member is employed.
Families below 200% of the poverty line would pay no fees; families above that level would pay on a sliding scale that never exceeds 7% of family income, no matter how many children they enroll.

Programs would be required to run full working days (at least 10 hours) and full calendar years, respond to families' schedules including nonstandard hours, and offer both center-based and home-based options.

The federal government would cover 80% of costs for low-income children, 50% for others, and 100% for children of migrant and seasonal farmworkers and for children in tribes and Native Hawaiian communities.

Child care staff and family child care providers would get a collective process, through their unions, to set wages, benefits, hours, and minimum working conditions, plus career-ladder training and compensation requirements tied to federal standards.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear most of the cost, under an open-ended appropriation of 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dollar cap. Families above 200% of the poverty line would pay sliding-scale fees up to 7% of income. States and localities would be barred from cutting their existing child care spending to offset the new money, and part of the non-federal share could come from employer or union contributions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; higher-income families pay fees

drawbacks.text: The core program is an open-ended entitlement with 'such sums as may be necessary' appropriated and no capped spending limit, so the total federal cost would depend entirely on enrollment and would not be fixed in the bill itself.

All programs receiving funds would have to meet new national program standards, facility codes, and compensation requirements, which would raise operating costs for small centers and home-based providers and could push some out of the program.

The bill directs sponsors to bargain with unions over wages, benefits, and working conditions for providers and staff, a significant added labor-cost and administrative obligation on top of the direct program spending.

Because every provider in a service area must guarantee placements, the bill relies on prime sponsors' capacity to expand supply quickly; families above the fee-free threshold would still pay up to 7% of income, a real cost for middle-income households.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary working families, the benefits are large and direct: guaranteed affordable care for children from six weeks to school age, at zero cost below 200% of the poverty line and a hard 7%-of-income cap above it, plus better pay and standards for the workforce that provides the care. The honest counterweight is that the bill wrote itself a blank check — no capped appropriation and no cost estimate in the record — so the fiscal commitment would have been enormous and open-ended, and the national standards and bargaining requirements would have imposed real compliance costs on the mostly small providers who deliver care. The design borrows heavily from Head Start and the military child care program, which have track records, but scaling that model to every child in the country had not been costed or tested in this record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on April 27, 2021, together with Senators Markey, Booker, Sanders, and Wyden.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions that same day.
Seven senators cosponsored the bill: six of 48 Senate Democrats and one of the two independents.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no committee report, and no floor vote; the last entry is the April 27, 2021 referral.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without ever coming up for a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the existing child care market, its providers, and their current fee and wage structures continued unchanged, and no new open-ended federal child care spending was created. Families with young children got none of the guaranteed affordable care the bill would have provided, and child care workers got none of the wage and bargaining rights it would have established.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no new federal child care spending

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Universal Child Care and Early Learning Act and recruited Senate cosponsors.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee from April 2021 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred. All seven cosponsors were Senate Democrats or the chamber's one independent supporter, and no Republican signed on, so the bill had no bipartisan path out of committee.

industries.industry: Child care and early learning providers (centers and home-based)
industries.note: Federal money would flow permanently through prime sponsors to providers — including for-profit and nonprofit agencies, schools, and family child care networks — making them the delivery channel for universal publicly funded care, while new national standards, wage requirements, and union bargaining duties would raise their operating costs.

industries.industry: Child care and early learning workforce
industries.note: Workers would get a collective process through their unions to set wages, benefits, hours, and working conditions, plus career-ladder training and compensation levels tied to federal standards — higher pay for a workforce that is predominantly low-wage women.

The bill allows the non-federal share of program costs to be paid through employer or union contributions, and reliably available child care stabilizes employees with young children; unions also gain a formal role in setting the workforce's wages and conditions.
